newsitem.title: USA: Calif. prison population projections cut--report.
newsitem.headline: Calif. prison population projections cut--report.

text.p: California prison officials on Friday said the state prison population would grow to over 181,700 in the year 2000, less than had been previously projected.
The prison population will rise from its current 144,000 inmates to 181,734 in 2000, the state Department of Corrections said in a report.
The department said, however, that the prison population growth rate was slowing to 6.4 percent a year against an earlier projection of 9.2 percent per year.
By contrast, the Department of Corrections said earlier this year that it expected the prison population to reach 203,593 in 2000.

Despite the slowing growth rate, the Department of Corrections said the state would need to house an addition 10,500 felons per year. The department said the state would run out of housing capacity when the prison population surpasses 177,000.
By 2001, the state will need four to five new prisons. To keep up with the population growth, two new prisons would need to be built each year after 2001.
California's prison population was projected to skyrocket as a direct result of "three strikes" legislation, which increases sentences for repeat offenders.

But Friday, state prison officials said "three strikes" was less of a factor on prison population growth than expected. State officials said judges were generally setencing felons to less time in prison than anticipated.
Even though population growth rates were slowing, prison officials said they would lobby the state Legislature next year to approve large bond issues to build new prisons.
"The story hasn't changed that much," said J.P. Tremblay, assistant secretary of the state's Youth and Adult Correctional Agency. "More prisons will need to be built."
In September, Tremblay said his agency would likely seek the authorization to sell up to $2 billion of lease revenue bonds to build new prison facilities.
Given the new prison population growth estimates, Tremblay said the agency's $2 billion figure may have to be revised.
